# Practical Exercise: Uniformity trials 2 (Extension) 

This exercise is useful for the following courses:

- 161.222;
- 161.228;
- and general revision on experimental design topics.

## Aims of this practical exercise


In this exercise you will:

- fit and validate linear models using factors,
- determine what changes need to be made to the linear models.

It builds on the [base exercise](https://r-resources.massey.ac.nz/practicals/uniformity1.html) which you are assumed to have completed.


## Before you undertake this exercise...

You will need to make sure several packages are ready for use in this exercise:


```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(ggfortify)
library(agridat)
```

##  Description of a uniformity trial (same as described in the base exercise)


Uniformity trials are conducted to assure researchers that the raw material to be used as experimental units is either homogeneous, or if it is not homogeneous, then how the proposed experimental units differ.

The most common use of uniformity trials  has been for agricultural research, but they could be used for considerably more contexts.

One benefit of understanding how an area of land differs, perhaps in its fertility, could be to establish the shape and size of areas to use as experimental units.

For the purposes of this exercise, we are only interested in understanding if and perhaps how an area varies.


### An example

We use the same data as before. Get the data ready to use:


```{r}
data(baker.strawberry.uniformity, package="agridat")
Trial1 <- baker.strawberry.uniformity  |>
filter(trial == "T1")|> glimpse()
```

That was unnecessary if you are continuing this extension exercise straight after the base exercise, but it is always a good idea to remind yourself of the data's structure.

## The Extra Models... 

The `row` and `col` variables were fitted as numeric. Convert to factors and re-fit the model. Call it `Trial1.lm3`

```{r}
Trial1.lm3 <- lm(yield~ as.factor(row) + as.factor(col), data=Trial1)

summary(Trial1.lm3)
```

```{r}
plot(Trial1.lm3)
```


Use the `anova()` command to investigate the fit of this model.


Q: Does it make a difference to any of your previous conclusions? 

```{r}
anova(Trial1.lm3)

anova(Trial1.lm1, Trial1.lm3)

anova(Trial1.lm2, Trial1.lm3)

anova(Trial1.lm1, Trial1.lm2, Trial1.lm3)
```

A: this new model does seem to improve on the initial model's column importance, but not those of the rows.
